I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01295

Shaykh Ahmad remained for some twenty years at Najaf and Karbalâ, the Shiite holy places in Iraq. In 1209/1794 a severe epidemic brought that stay to an end. He returned home, but less than four years later, in 1212/1797, came back on a new pilgrimage. He spent the next seven years traveling back and forth around Basra, frequently changing his place of residence to escape the crowds drawn to him by his growing reputation.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01296

In 1221/1806 he made a decision that would have profound consequences for Iranian Imamism: to undertake a pilgrimage to Mashhad, to the shrine of the Eighth Imam, 'Alî Rezâ. It would lead to his first stay in Iran of roughly ten years. As so often happens in Iran, one plans a visit of a few weeks and ends up remaining for years. Setting out from Basra in 1221/1806 with his family and a few friends, he followed a route—hardly the shortest by modern standards—that took him through Yazd, in southeastern Iran, on the road to Kerman.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01297

Many scholars were living in Yazd at that time, and all welcomed Shaykh Ahmad with exceptional warmth and reverence. Not a day passed without lengthy scholarly discussions, in which he was asked to comment on and resolve difficult questions. On Fridays and feast days he was requested to lead the prayers. Before long it became impossible for him to leave Yazd. The most he could obtain was permission to continue his pilgrimage to Mashhad, on the promise that he would return.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01298

There he received the same welcome. Once back in Yazd, he remained for about five years, occupied with teaching and with composing a multitude of treatises in answer to the questions put to him. His reputation spread so widely throughout Iran that the sovereign, Fath 'Alî-Shâh Qâdjâr, wrote him a moving letter and, so eager was he to speak with the shaykh, offered to come to Yazd himself. In the end Shaykh Ahmad went to Tehran, where the ruler urged him to settle permanently.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01299
But the shaykh preferred to return to Yazd. Soon afterward, apparently following a command received from the First Imam in a dream, he decided to return to Iraq.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01300

This time his journey took him through Isfahan, then the “navel of Iran,” the “dome of Islam,” or what we might now call the country's spiritual and intellectual capital. Once again he received an extraordinary welcome from scholars and the heads of the philosophical schools. His books were eagerly sought, copied, and recopied. After forty days he resumed his journey.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01301

The governor of Kermânshâh, then the royal prince Mohammad 'Alî Mîrzâ Dawlatshâh, came out to meet him, accompanied by all the scholars and dignitaries, as far as four farsakhs—some twenty-five kilometers—from the city. The situation he had encountered in Yazd repeated itself. Shaykh Ahmad remained in Kermânshâh for two years, during which people from every quarter sought his teaching and advice. Then, wishing to make the pilgrimage to Mecca, he set out again, having firmly promised to return (1231/1816).
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01302

And indeed, once the pilgrimage was complete, Shaykh Ahmad reappeared in Kermânshâh in 1234/1819. This new period in Iran would last about five years. The prince and the people welcomed him with the same enthusiasm as before. Because the city lay on the pilgrimage route to Mashhad, he could meet many fellow scholars as they passed through.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01303
But now a succession of disasters unfolded.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01304

First the prince-governor died. Then came a devastating drought, followed by floods. A quarter of the city lay in ruins. An epidemic broke out and spread across Iran. Shaykh Ahmad and his companions set out for Mashhad by a route roughly corresponding to the one used today: Qazwîn, Qomm, Tehran, where he visited the shrine of Shâh 'Abdol-'Azîm, then Shâhrûd, Neyshâpûr, and Mashhad.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01305

At every stage the epidemic seemed to grow worse. From Mashhad the little caravan headed south again toward Yazd, passing through the oases of the central desert: Torbat, then Tabas. Beyond Tabas the road was infested with Baluch bandits, so the governor provided an escort of cavalry and infantry. Shaykh Ahmad thus entered Yazd preceded, this time, by an entirely unexpected military procession. He remained there only three months.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01306

At Isfahan the reception was overwhelming, triumphant. It included not just the governor, scholars, and dignitaries, but the whole population: old and young, men and women. The shaykh was asked to lead the prayer in the royal mosque (Masjad-e Shâh). The rows of worshippers spilled out onto the great maydân, the celebrated square of Shâh 'Abbâs. One shaykh, fond of statistics, counted as many as sixteen thousand people there on a single evening (pp. 211–214).
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01307

It is against this background of widespread reverence and enthusiasm—evidence that Shiite religious consciousness recognized itself in Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î and his teaching—that we must judge the regrettable incident at Qazwîn. Western writers have sometimes claimed that Shaykh Ahmad “was excommunicated by the mojtaheds.” This language is entirely inappropriate and wholly out of proportion to what actually happened. It translates the event through a particular Western way of seeing things, speaking as though there were a Church in a setting where no central teaching office or binding dogmatic authority exists.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01308

Nor was there ever an assembly of mojtaheds to consider the matter. The takfîr pronounced at Qazwîn—the declaration that someone is an unbeliever—was a personal, private initiative of Mullâ Mohammad Taqî Barghânî. It neither had nor could have had anything like the meaning or force of a decision by a Church council. Shaykh Sarkâr Âghâ's account brings out both the historical and the human dimensions of this affair particularly well (pp. 190–202).
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01309

First there were reasons that were human, all too human, and easy enough to understand. The welcome given everywhere to Shaykh Ahmad and his teaching, including at Qazwîn, wounded the pride of certain individuals. Something like a wind of spiritual renewal was blowing through Shiite consciousness. The distress of these injured vanities was joined by fear: an established authority was being shaken, a privileged position put at risk.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01310

Second, Mullâ Barghânî was far from being a leading figure. He was a preacher. He had indeed bestowed on himself the title a'lam, “the foremost scholar” of Qazwîn, but neither his writings nor his sermons had persuaded his colleagues to share that opinion. Of those who happened to attend the majlis he convened, only four or five joined him in his takfîr, and even they were neither mojtaheds nor scholars of particular eminence.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01311

Tonkâbûnî himself, who can hardly be suspected of favoring Shaykh Ahmad, is obliged to acknowledge this. Neither then nor afterward did Mullâ Barghânî's takfîr command anything resembling general agreement. More telling still, his own son, Shaykh Ja'far Yazdî, who had suffered greatly because of his father's conduct, later spent many years in Kerman on terms of close friendship with the Shaykhis.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01312

The question discussed at the small gathering hastily convened on Molla Barghani’s initiative was that of ma'âd jismânî, the bodily resurrection. I have dealt at length elsewhere with the Shaykhi teaching on this essential religious doctrine, so I shall only touch on it briefly here. Through its account of the human being's fourfold bodily nature and its conception of a subtle spiritual body (jism hûrqalyî, caro spiritualis), Shaykhism stands at an equal distance from the philosophers and the literalist theologians. (For Molla Barghani to claim that Shaykh Ahmad's teaching on this point agreed with that of Molla Sadra Shirazi, he must have misunderstood the writings of both.) When the Shaykhis say that "the elemental body does not return," they mean that the "materialism" of theologians who cling to the literal meaning of scripture leads them into absurdities that amount to blasphemy.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01313

To Molla Barghani, however, this understanding of bodily resurrection was tantamount to denying it. He had an excuse: his education had done little to prepare him for metaphysical questions. But in that case, Sarkar Agha observes, those who lack the capacity to understand the wisdom (hikmat) taught by the Prophet and the holy Imams would do better not to discuss it.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01314

At heart, the entire affair was merely a symptom of the deeper unease whose causes we noted at the beginning of this account. The Shaykhis regard the hostility of the religious jurists (foqahâ) toward hikmat ilâhîya—divine wisdom, encompassing philosophy and spiritual theosophy—as a contradiction of the traditions and teachings that Shiism has inherited from the Prophet and the Imams. In a letter written later to a friend, Shaykh 'Abdul-Wahhab Qazvini, Shaykh Ahmad pointed out that his doctrine of the "resurrection body" could appeal to the most explicit statements by authorities such as the Sixth Imam, Ja'far Sadiq, Nasir Tusi, 'Allameh Hilli, and even Majlisi himself (p. 198). Unfortunately, his opponents were unable to rise to the level at which such a discussion properly belonged. Shaykhism, by contrast, breathed new life into the questions of cosmogony and eschatology: the origin of the world and its final destiny, Mabdâ' and Ma'âd.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01315

What, precisely, did the man who initiated this takfîr—this declaration that another Muslim was an unbeliever—stand to gain? Certainly, today its immediate significance is no longer the same for either side; nor, for that matter, is the significance of such a declaration in general. Even at the time, it failed to win the support of a majority, let alone acquire any binding religious authority.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01316

Yet it was shamefully exploited to stir up unrest and to give free rein to resentments that could not be openly acknowledged. Most serious of all was the decision to thrust into public controversy questions that the public was in no position to understand. Among the poorer and less educated people, this created an opinion about the "Shaykhis" that was wholly uninformed about the issues involved, yet all the more ready to provoke disturbances. We shall see this hostility at work, unfortunately, on several occasions in Kerman.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01317

After this painful incident, Shaykh Ahmad spent another year in Iran, at Kermanshah, before returning to Karbala, where he hoped to spend the rest of his life. Molla Barghani then began writing letter after letter to those jurists in Iraq whom he thought he might win over. The intrigues multiplied scandalously. Forged documents were even produced to alarm the Ottoman governor, Dawud Pasha, who was already deeply hostile to Shiism. These discreditable maneuvers eventually created such a dangerous situation that Shaykh Ahmad decided to withdraw with his family to Mecca. They set out on the journey for the last time.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01318

But when they were three stages from Medina, the shaykh developed a fever and departed this world on 21 Dhu'l-Qa'da 1241 AH (28 June 1826). He was buried in Medina, in the cemetery of Baqî' rafî', near the graves of four of the Shiite Imams and the Bayt al-Ahzân, the House of Sorrows, with which the poignant memory of Fatima remains associated.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01319

Thus ended the earthly life of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i, a life devoted, as he himself had wished, entirely to the veneration of what he regarded as the purest essence of Shiism. His influence upon its spiritual life was undoubtedly immense, and the possibilities opened by his work are far from exhausted.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01320

There is something curious here. On the one hand, Shaykh Ahmad cannot be traced back to any particular spiritual master among his contemporaries. On the other, although he had children and grandchildren, no members of his family line are now known by name.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01321

We can speak only of his spiritual descendants: those called the Shaykhis, who are numerous in Iran and Iraq and are also found in India. It should also be noted (p. 217) that in Kuwait and several cities of Azerbaijan there are groups which, although they do not call themselves Shaykhis, trace their spiritual ancestry to Shaykh Ahmad and Sayyed Kazem. Conversely, there are others who adopt the Shaykhi name although their teachings bear little resemblance to those of the two masters.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01322

This confusion has more serious dimensions. Among the students (tâleb) who gathered around Shaykh Ahmad and Sayyed Kazem were some who were not, for all that, Shaykhi disciples (tâleb shaykhis). Nevertheless, the improvised ideas put forward by these students have been attributed to the two masters themselves. To create and perpetuate this confusion, people have even appealed to the authority of Khwansari, the great historian of leading figures in the Islamic world, whose deeply respectful and admiring words about Shaykh Ahmad we have already noted.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01323

In fact, his Arabic text has been strikingly misunderstood. This misreading gave rise to the opinion, which has influenced some Orientalists, that Babism "came out of" Shaykhism. What we shall say later about the "fourth rokn" will show decisively that, if this proposition is true at all, it is only in the strict sense of "coming out": that is, leaving Shaykhism, placing oneself outside it, breaking away from it.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01324

In the end, Sarkar Agha concludes, "there are we, who are called the Shaykhis and who are disciples of the Shaykh because we find in his teaching the whole tradition of Shiism, with all the possibilities contained within it." He adds, with no small courage: "This name was given to us; we did not choose it.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01325

"But we accept it as a title of honor precious above all others, because in its true meaning and content it is, for us, equivalent to the name Moslimûn—Muslims. And because we are distinguished in this way through our attachment to our eminent Shaykh, we are sometimes described as a minority. That designation, too, is a source of pride to us, for even in the time of the holy Imams their companions and friends were never anything but a minority."
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01326

What, indeed, is a Shiite? "The word existed already in the Prophet's lifetime, to designate those who professed love and devotion toward the Imam and separated themselves from those who had separated themselves from him. That was how they were recognized—not by the fact that they observed prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and so forth.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01327

"Yet even then, and ever since, they could always be counted on the fingers of one's hands. Many traditions (akhbâr) praise this minority. Let those who today heap suspicion and slander upon us know that they are treating us just as people treated the companions and friends of the holy Imams in their day. When, in the time of Imam Ja'far Sadiq, these companions came to complain that people called them Râfizis, Ja'faris, and other such names, the Imam reassured them, saying: Do not grieve; be patient. From the beginning of the world, ordinary people have always treated the Friends of God in this way" (pp. 221–222).
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01328
These proud words deserve to be quoted here, for they convey a whole spiritual atmosphere more vividly than any commentary could.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01329

As for the writings of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i, they form a vast body of work whose study is indispensable to anyone wishing to penetrate the deeper mysteries of Shiite thought. Thanks to Sarkar Agha's work, we now possess a systematic and comprehensive catalogue. It lists no fewer than 132 titles, all Shaykh Ahmad's recorded writings being in Arabic. The true number is higher, since many titles refer to collections containing as many as ten or more individual treatises (risâla).
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01330

We must also remember that a considerable number of works have been lost: the shaykh did not keep copies of the treatises he wrote at the request of his correspondents and those who consulted him. Moreover, his library was kept in Karbala, in the house of his disciple and successor Sayyed Kazem, and that house was pillaged twice.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01331

The catalogue is systematically arranged into nine sections: theosophy; Shiite doctrine; religious addresses and sermons; law; jurisprudence; Quranic commentaries; practical philosophy; literature; and collections (II, pp. 8–85). Approximately seventeen treatises remain unpublished. All the others appeared in lithographed editions, which are unfortunately now quite old. Particularly worth recalling are Shaykh Ahmad's extensive and highly individual commentaries on two works by Molla Sadra Shirazi. These are essential for understanding how Shaykhi theosophy relates to the "Eastern theosophy" (hikmat mashriqîya) of Suhrawardi as interpreted by Molla Sadra.
I. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î (1241/1826)
passage-en-01332

The Sharh al-Ziyârat al-jâmi'a is an extensive commentary on a text of "spiritual pilgrimage" honoring the Twelve Imams. With the Shaykhis, we may regard it as Shaykh Ahmad's most precious work: a veritable comprehensive statement of Shiite theosophy. The Fawâ'id ("Teachings") and the expanded version prepared by the author himself contain philosophical foundations of great importance. A large collection of ninety-nine treatises—actually more, for the reason already given—was published under the title Jawâmi' al-Kalim. We must reserve a more detailed discussion of all this for another occasion.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01333
Chapter II The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
en-book-6-ch-2-s1
1. Sayyed Kazem Reshti (1212/1798–1259/1843)
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01334

The Shaykhi community enjoyed the good fortune of being led, after Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i, by a succession of figures as remarkable for their strength and nobility of character as for their truly extraordinary scholarly productivity.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01335

Until now, anyone wishing to write the biography of the disciple whom Shaykh Ahmad expressly designated as his nâ'ib, his deputy and successor, had only incomplete sources at hand. The first was Sayyed Kazem's own account of his trials, especially his controversies and disputes with people whose names would otherwise have been forgotten. Further research has now enabled Sarkar Agha to discover two treatises (risâla) written by students of Sayyed Kazem, containing at last the material needed for a proper biography. We shall draw from them a very brief account.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01336

Sayyed Kazem belonged to a noble family of Hosayni sayyeds—that is, descendants of the Third Imam—originally from Medina, which had settled in Iran two generations earlier. His grandfather, Sayyed Ahmad, had fled Medina during an outbreak of plague and taken refuge in Rasht, in the region southwest of the Caspian Sea. He settled there and established a family. His son, Sayyed Qasem, was born there, married there, and became one of Rasht's leading citizens. It was in the same city that Sayyed Kazem was born, in 1212 AH (1798).
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01337

His dreamy, contemplative childhood reveals dispositions strikingly similar to those we encountered in Shaykh Ahmad's own early life. A tutor was appointed to teach him the outward, or exoteric, sciences (zâhira). But the young man was consumed by two desires: to travel far from home and to be initiated into the higher forms of knowledge. Unfortunately, his family saw matters differently. Once again, a series of "initiatory dreams" strengthened his resolve and hastened his decision.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01338

One fact deserves particular attention. It was Fatima, the Prophet's daughter and a central focus of Shiite devotion, who appeared to the young Kazem in a dream and revealed to him the existence of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i, the extraordinary nature of the man, and finally the place where he could be found: Yazd. We have already described the circumstances in which Shaykh Ahmad came to Yazd and remained there until 1229 AH (1814). Sayyed Kazem, then about fifteen years old, managed somehow to leave home and reach the city. His hopes and expectations were fully answered. He "committed every resource of his soul and heart" to absorbing the shaykh's teaching. From then on he became his inseparable companion and closest confidant. The shaykh was accustomed to saying: "My son Kazem understands me, but nobody else understands me" (pp. 147–148).
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01339

It was during the journey that took Shaykh Ahmad back toward the holy places, when he made his final stay at Kermanshah after the unhappy episode at Qazvin, that he advised his disciple to settle in Karbala. Sayyed Kazem appears indeed to have established himself there at about that time, devoting himself entirely to his twofold task of teaching and spiritual guidance.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01340

Yet he must have returned several times to Iran, to his native Rasht, as we learn from one of his letters to the shaykh, unfortunately undated. During his years in Iraq he certainly suffered attacks and mistreatment at the hands of a small number of envious and troublesome individuals. But these hardships were offset by the friendship of eminent scholars who testified to his greatness of soul, the breadth of his learning and spiritual gifts, and the intensity of his inner life.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01341

Nothing better conveys the impression he made upon those around him than the words of Mahmud Alusi, then the mufti of Baghdad and author of the Maqâmât alûsîya: "If the Sayyed had lived in an age when it was possible for a prophet (nabî) to be sent, I would have been the first to believe in him. For everything required—profound knowledge, moral conduct, sound doctrine, and spiritual gifts—is present in him."
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01342

In 1258 AH (1842), the people of Karbala rose in revolt against supporters of the Ottoman government. Terrible scenes of repression, pillage, and massacre followed. The sanctuaries and the Sayyed's house miraculously served as places of refuge. Afterward, however, the attacks against him—whose underlying motives are not difficult to guess—grew more intense. Eventually he decided to absent himself on a long pilgrimage to the sanctuary of the Kazimayn and then to Samarra.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01343

But as he prepared to leave, he had a premonition that this would be his final journey. We have the testimony of Mirza Hasan Tabib, a distinguished physician and disciple of Sayyed Kazem, who recounts their last conversation:
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01344
"At the time of this journey, the revered Sayyed came to see me and said: 'Janab Mirza! Will you accompany me on the pilgrimage?'
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01345
"'I fear that will not be possible,' I answered, 'for I have several patients whom I am treating.'
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01346
"'Give them their prescriptions,' he said, 'and be sure to come with me. I have a feeling this will be my last journey.'
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01347
"'Agha!' I cried, 'may my life be devoted to you! God will not allow it. By divine grace, you are in perfect health and will remain so.'
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01348
"'Janab Mirza,' he replied, 'I know something that you do not know. Remember what I have just told you. Do not speak of it to anyone'" (pp. 153–154).
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01349

In fact, when Sayyed Kazem reached Baghdad on his return from Samarra, the Ottoman governor, Najib Pasha, who had applauded the killing and pillage at Karbala, invited him to visit and lavished every kind of honor and respect upon him. Nevertheless, he had a cup of "bad coffee" served to him. His friends hurriedly carried the Sayyed back to Karbala, where he died two days later, on the night of 11 Dhu'l-Hijja 1259 AH (1843). He was buried very near the sanctuary of Imam Hosayn, his distant ancestor.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01350

Through Sayyed Kazem, the spiritual succession of the shaykhs belonging to the silsila shaykhîya—the Shaykhi chain of transmission—was secured. In the ijâzat, or formal authorization to teach and transmit knowledge, which he granted to Agha Mohammad Sharif Kermani, he mentions four such authorizations received from his own spiritual masters (mashâyekh). The authority of the fourth overshadowed the other three, for it came from Shaykh Ahmad himself.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01351

Speaking of the relationship between the shaykh and his successor, Khwansari writes: "They were a single spirit manifested in two bodies." He emphasizes that, among his many disciples, Shaykh Ahmad designated no one but Sayyed Kazem as his nâ'ib al-manâb, his duly qualified representative and the spiritual leader of his companions and fellow disciples. Admittedly, Khwansari's testimony concerns only their outward relationship, for his great book sometimes shows that he had only an imperfect knowledge of the shaykhs and had little personal contact with them. Nevertheless, his testimony helps place this historical point beyond dispute (pp. 158–160).
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01352

The writings left by Sayyed Kazem (II, pp. 86–167) are likewise considerable. The catalogue lists no fewer than 172 titles—and the real number is even greater: entry 130 contains sixty-three separate treatises; entry 144 contains thirty-three; and entry 152 contains no fewer than eighty! Unfortunately, many of these writings seem to have been lost beyond recovery. As already mentioned, the Sayyed's house in Karbala, where his descendants lived and his library was kept, was pillaged twice. A substantial number of Shaykh Ahmad's autograph manuscripts disappeared at the same time, since his library was also preserved in Sayyed Kazem's house (p. 157).
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01353

Fortunately, Sayyed Kazem had himself compiled a catalogue of his own works and those of the Shaykh, accompanying each entry with a short description of the book's contents. Thanks to this care, we can estimate the number of missing works at around sixty. Some thirty-five writings, on the other hand, still exist but remain unpublished; about fifteen of his works in all are in Persian. The others were printed at various dates, and copies have become rare. Much work will be required to recover this body of writing and thought, and to trace in detail how Sayyed Kazem developed and extended the ideas of Shaykh Ahmad. His commentaries on certain sermons (khotbat) and other texts attributed to the Imams reveal his particular aptitude for the highest reaches of speculative spiritual philosophy.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
en-book-6-ch-2-s2
2. Shaykh Hajj Mohammad Karim-Khan Kermani (1225/1809–1288/1870)
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01354

This shaykh was born in Kerman on 18 Moharram 1225 AH (1809) and died on 22 Sha'ban 1288 AH (1870) at Teh-Rud, three stages from Kerman, while making a pilgrimage to Karbala. His life seems short when measured against his astonishing achievement. He left no fewer than 278 works—some substantial volumes, others brief treatises—preserved in Kerman and for the most part still unpublished. He was an exceptional figure, whose learning embraced the whole spiritual culture of his setting and his age. The comparison that naturally comes to mind is with the universal minds produced by the European Renaissance.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01355
Two great features define the course of his life.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01356

The first was a conviction that he shared with Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i: the immense body of traditions transmitted from the holy Imams contains a complete spiritual philosophy, a whole body of knowledge concerning this world and the other worlds. Those responsible for the impoverishment of Shiism, in his view, were precisely those who turned to these traditions only to justify legal decisions or ritual practices. What was needed instead was direct study of this inherited body of teaching, without any intermediary authority.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01357

This meant breaking with every legalistic conception of Islam. The break became all the more decisive because the seeker was now called to enter into a direct, personal dialogue with his Imams. We must always keep this in mind if we are to understand the difficulties the Shaykhis encountered at the hands of the official religious establishment.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01358

The second defining event came when Mohammad Karim-Khan, at the age of seventeen, first heard of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i's teaching in Kerman itself. From this discovery came, one might say, the dazzling illumination that lit up his entire life. It happened in 1826. The date coincides with Shaykh Ahmad's final stay at Kermanshah and his return to the Shiite holy places in Iraq; it was at this time, as we have seen, that he instructed Sayyed Kazem to establish himself in Karbala.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01359

Here again, Sarkar Agha's research has borne fruit. Among the mass of papers left by Mohammad Karim-Khan, he discovered several pages in the shaykh's own hand containing nothing less than the outline of an autobiography, reaching back into his childhood. It had been intended as the introduction to a work written in Arabic. Sarkar Agha provides a Persian translation (pp. 76–92). The document is so interesting that we hope, as in the case of Shaykh Ahmad's autobiography, to publish a complete French translation elsewhere. Here we can draw attention to only a few features.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01360

Through his father, Ebrahim-Khan, the shaykh belonged to the reigning imperial family. From his own account we learn how his father founded the great religious college in Kerman that still bears the name Madrasa-ye Ebrâhîmî, furnishing it with a fine library that grew richer year after year. Ebrahim-Khan installed his son there, giving him a separate residence and his own household staff. The young man was thus free to devote himself entirely to his studies, sheltered from worries and intrigues, and ideally placed to attend the lessons of every visiting master.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01361

His method of study was uncompromising: for every book he read, he wrote a book of his own. By the age of fourteen, he had already composed a treatise on grammar and another on logic. He then turned to the sciences, and afterward to the fine arts. Until his death, his father never ceased encouraging this almost feverish appetite for learning.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01362

We can readily imagine the shock that the arrival of Mohammad Isma'il Kuhbena'i, a direct disciple of Shaykh Ahmad, must have brought to this young man whose hunger for knowledge was so consuming. Mohammad Isma'il came to Kerman and stayed for a year. At first, it seems, he took little interest in this privileged young scholar. Then a particular trait of the young man's character, reported to him by others, attracted his attention, and he wished to meet him.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01363

When Mohammad Karim-Khan heard him speak of Shaykh Ahmad, and when Mohammad Isma'il gave him a glimpse of the broad outlines of the shaykh's spiritual philosophy and understanding of the Imams, his vocation was settled. He wanted to hear of nothing else.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01364

Consequently, when his new friend had to return to Karbala, Mohammad Karim-Khan felt such an overwhelming longing that he overcame every obstacle. He too set out for Karbala, where, for eight months, he was an accepted disciple of Sayyed Kazem, already renowned as Shaykh Ahmad's successor. Sayyed Kazem was then twenty-eight years old; Mohammad Karim-Khan was about seventeen. The meeting of these two young men, both burning with the same spiritual enthusiasm, proved decisive for the future of Shaykhism and the spiritual life of Iran.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01365

Pressing family obligations recalled Mohammad Karim-Khan to Kerman. Four years later, however, he returned to Karbala and spent another two years under Sayyed Kazem's guidance. In his teacher he saw the "mirror" of Shaykh Ahmad, just as he himself had now become Sayyed Kazem's "mirror." During this period he also made the pilgrimage to Mecca.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01366

Then Sayyed Kazem instructed him to depart. He accompanied his disciple beyond the outskirts of Karbala and, at their farewell, said simply: "Return to Persia. From now on, you have no need of anyone among the olamâ," the religious scholars (p. 74).
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01367

The autobiography also gives us testimony of exceptional interest for understanding religious experience. Like Shaykh Ahmad and Sayyed Kazem, Mohammad Karim-Khan—especially in his youth—was granted visions in which the events he experienced gave symbolic form to the underlying patterns of Shiite spiritual consciousness. Even before his birth, his mother had experienced symbolic and prophetic dreams; one has the impression that her son's visionary experiences were, in a sense, a continuation of them.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01368

We cannot examine these visions at length here, but several deserve particular mention. There was an encounter in a visionary dream with the Eighth Imam. In other visions, the familiar image of an object descending from heaven reappears in a different form: a mysterious device that enables the dreamer to ascend to heaven. Finally, and above all, there was a vision of the Ninth Imam, Mohammad Jawad (also called Taqi), which amounted to a personal initiation.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01369
Following this experience, the shaykh says that he made a resolution, which he expresses in these words:
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01370

"From that time onward, I gave my attention to searching out hidden things. I came to perceive the holy Imams in my mind, to see them inwardly, and I felt myself guided by them. Henceforth, whenever I sought knowledge, I turned directly to them and to no one else. I profess nothing that is not founded upon them. I give my unquestioning allegiance (taqlîd) to no one else. All my knowledge comes from my inner vision, from the teaching of the Imams as it guides my spiritual search. From nothing else" (p. 83).
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01371

The same spiritual fearlessness, inspired by a direct relationship with the unseen world of the holy Imams, is already foreshadowed in a prophetic dream from his adolescence. He sees a strange apparatus rising toward the heights of heaven. It has a series of steps or platforms, but most people are content merely to take their places upon them. One of his companions tries to reach the summit and fails. In the intuitive certainty of the dream, the young Karim-Khan knows that whoever reaches the top will set the whole apparatus in motion and become the guide of everyone else. He succeeds in climbing to the summit and takes hold of the controls.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01372

Such a dream gives us a sense of the strength of character that Shiite spirituality can impart to those who live it as fully and exemplarily as these shaykhs did, acknowledging no authority other than the inner authority of the Imams.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01373

This pure inner authority would henceforth guide and inspire a labor that resulted in a body of work of overwhelming proportions. It is impossible here to follow the details of its development. Yet we should call attention to a few of the maxims that conclude the autobiography, addressed to the reader of the book for which it was intended to serve as a preface.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01374
They reveal the exceptional strength of a personality that drew its very strength from the Shiite faith as he understood and practiced it:
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01375
"I have turned everything upside down, examined and tested everything, and have no aim other than to make the truth manifest.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01376

"The two Angels merely write down what a human being dictates to them through his words, his thoughts, his tongue, and his other bodily organs. Beyond them, God perceives the secrets of our innermost consciousness, and on the Day of Resurrection He will bring forth the book in which they are recorded.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01377
"Do not offer as an argument: 'We found our fathers following this path or that.' Perhaps your father knew nothing about it.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01378

"Beware of finding comfort in agreement with beasts or with those who have lost their way. For the First Imam said: 'You will never know the sweetness of faith unless you keep company with the few and flee from the multitude. Whoever deserves the name of human being does not keep company with wild beasts.'
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01379

"Know that insofar as you love such creatures, you become like them. A human being takes the very form of what he loves. You will be resurrected in their likeness, for if someone loves a stone, God will resurrect that person in the form of that stone.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01380

"Whoever lacks the Spirit of faith is dead. Avoid sitting and talking with the dead, for what teaching can be expected from corpses? If you happen to come into contact with them, you must purify yourself.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01381
"If you have been tested as I have been, let only your outward person maintain such relationships, never your heart.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01382

"Do not say: 'Other people do not speak this way; this person or that disapproves.' For I too am one of those 'others.' And you too possess authority, if God approves of you in His Book, the Prophet in his sonna—his exemplary practice—and the Imams in their transmitted teachings (akhbâr)" (pp. 85–91).
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01383

The question of the ijâzât, the authorizations received by Hajj Mohammad Karim-Khan, deserves closer attention. He received many of them, notably from Molla Hosayn Ganjavi and Agha Mohammad Sharif Kermani. But naturally their importance is somewhat overshadowed by the two detailed authorizations he received from Sayyed Kazem himself.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01384

Curiously, because the preface to his great work Fasl al-Khitâb reproduces only the first two—his concern there being to emphasize the continuity in the transmission of the religious traditions (riwâyât)—certain people have claimed that he never received an ijâzat from Sayyed Kazem. Yet the texts of the two comprehensive authorizations granted by Sayyed Kazem are reproduced in the Tadhkarat al-Awliyâ (see above, note 38), and the autograph original, bearing the Sayyed's seal, is preserved in Kerman.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01385

This is hardly a recent controversy. For reasons upon which we need not dwell here, certain people were already raising the question during Mohammad Karim-Khan's lifetime. He himself had given them a decisive answer simply by producing the documents (pp. 74–75, 92–93).
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01386

This resolves one of the questions raised chiefly among certain groups in Azerbaijan to which we have already referred. Sometimes these groups regard themselves as belonging to the Shaykhi spiritual lineage (silsila shaykhîya); at other times they place themselves outside it, while still claiming to be disciples of Shaykh Ahmad and Sayyed Kazem.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01387

But another question concerns what Shaykhism regards as the "fourth pillar" of the Shiite religion, expressed in the term rokn-e râbi'. We shall attempt to give a brief account of this doctrine later (Chapter III). First, however, we must establish an important historical point.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01388

It has been claimed that the doctrine is found neither in Shaykh Ahmad nor in Sayyed Kazem, but was a "creation" of Mohammad Karim-Khan. This is the origin of the names Roknîyeh and Hâjj-Karîm-Khânî, sometimes given to his disciples, who indeed regard these designations with pride.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01389

This supposed objection can readily be answered in two ways. First, we can refer to the writings of the first two masters. Second, we can refer to two autograph documents written by Sayyed Kazem that settle the question definitively.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01390

Besides confirming Mohammad Karim-Khan's authority as successor, these two documents help us understand why he insisted so strongly and so persistently on teaching this doctrine. There should be no room for doubt, were it not for what Sarkar Agha deplores as "ordinary people's unwillingness to receive the higher teachings of the Imams."
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01391

As for Mohammad Karim-Khan's bibliography, it is assembled (II, pp. 168–305) under fifteen broad headings, covering the following subjects: theosophy; Shiite doctrine and religious controversy; religious addresses and sermons; Quranic commentaries; traditions (akhbâr) of the Imams; sources of religious law; jurisprudence; treatises on prayer and devotion; medicine; studies of light, optics, perspective, and mirrors; treatises on color and music; astronomy, mathematics, and the astrolabe; alchemy; dream interpretation and geomancy; calligraphy, poetry, and grammar; and responses to questions on various subjects.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01392

The catalogue contains 278 titles. As we have said, the actual number is higher, for the same reasons encountered in the earlier cases. Of these works, around fifty are in Persian, and barely fifty of the entire collection have ever been printed.
